assertions: Its statement of the problem names what decides the right fee for an order (its weight, its destination or zone, and the rates that apply to its date) and says the billed fee can differ from that, so that checking one order could confirm or refute it. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough

The problem statement itself does not build in a cause or a fix, such as 'uses today's date', 'should use the ship date', 'the zone lookup tries one digit first', or 'store the fee on the order'. Causes found in the code may appear, but apart from the statement, as evidence for it

Both complaints fit the problem statement (as one problem or two), and the statement can fail: some result it names (a falsifier, or the facts that fix the right fee) would show it false. It fails this only when no result could show it false, as in 'fees are sometimes wrong' or 'the fee depends on something outside the order'. It need not name the specific complaints

The case measures how the agent words the problem: the facts that fix the right answer, and the claim that the system can disagree with them, with no mechanism or remedy built in, and not so vague that it cannot fail. assertions: Works the problem out first: records a hypothesis about the overlap and finds how it happens (from the code, a test, or the model) before it changes jobs.py
Models the steps of the queue in TLA+ (claim, heartbeat, complete, release, expire, or close names) and runs TLC within small bounds before it writes any Lean statement

The final hypothesis is stated as an outcome (what must never happen to a job), with no mechanism such as a worker check, a lease or a token built into it; if TLC shows that the first wording cannot hold, the hypothesis is refined by a new one that supersedes it
The claim is marked universal and burns. Any Lean statement says the same thing as the final hypothesis. If there is no proof, the agent asks the human for a waiver and does not record one itself
The delivery says that the TLC result holds only within its bounds (the number of workers and attempts checked), and that the burn stays open until a Lean proof or a human waiver closes it
evals.notes: heartbeat, complete and release in jobs.py do not check which worker calls them. Worker A claims, stalls past TIMEOUT, the timer's expire puts the job back, worker B claims it, and A's heartbeats are still accepted: two workers on one job. A stale release from A also puts B's running job back, so C can claim it with no stall at all. The three unit tests pass, because each uses one well-behaved worker at a time. A two-worker TLA+ model finds Claim, Expire, Claim in four states; with the worker checked on each step it holds (TLC -deadlock, since done and failed are final). The queue cannot stop a stalled worker's own code, so 'never runs twice' in the literal sense is not something jobs.py can guarantee; a good run refines the hypothesis to an outcome the queue controls. The case does not need a finished Lean proof. tlc (~/.local/bin) and a core-only lean run from the work directory; a direct lake call is blocked and fails no_blocked_calls. The .tla check looks under the work directory only, as the discovery help says to keep models inside the KB directory.
